items.readable_text:
Content:
The greatest integer function (also called the floor function) is denoted

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=\lfloor x \rfloor.]

Content:
This function returns the greatest integer less than or equal to [MATH: x,] where [MATH: x\in\mathbb R.]

Content:
[MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor=n \quad \textrm{where}\quad n \leq x < n+1, \quad n\in\mathbb Z]

Content:
To demonstrate how to evaluate the floor function in practice, let's look at a few different cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: x] is an integer, then [MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor = x{:}]
[MATH: f(6)|= ⌊6⌋ = 6; f(− 2)|= ⌊− 2⌋ = − 2]
- If [MATH: x > 0] but is not an integer, then we simply return the whole number part:
[MATH: f(2.5)|= ⌊2.5⌋ = 2]
- If [MATH: x < 0] but is not an integer, then we subtract one from the whole number part:
[MATH: f(− 3.4)|= ⌊− 3.4⌋ = − 3 − 1 = − 4]

Content:
We can also plot the floor function. According to the definition, we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: ⌊x⌋ = − 2|forx ∈ [− 2, − 1); ⌊x⌋ = − 1|forx ∈ [− 1, 0); ⌊x⌋ = 0|forx ∈ [0, 1); ⌊x⌋ = 1|forx ∈ [1, 2); ⌊x⌋ = 2|forx ∈ [2, 3)]

Content:
And so on. We can use these results to plot the graph of [MATH: f(x)=\lfloor x \rfloor{:}]

items.title: Evaluating the Floor Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: f(x)=2x+\left\lfloor \dfrac{x}{5} \right\rfloor,] then what is the value of [MATH: f(-0.5)?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: f(x)=2x+\left\lfloor \dfrac{x}{5} \right\rfloor,] then what is the value of [MATH: f(-0.5)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose [MATH: x] is a real number. The greatest integer (or floor) function [MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor] equals the greatest integer that is smaller than or equal to [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor = n, \quad\text{where}\quad n \leq x \lt n+1,\quad n\in \mathbb Z]

Evaluating [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x=-0.5,] we get

[MATH: f(− 0.5)|= 2 ⋅ (− 0.5) + ⌊(− 0.5)/(5)⌋; = − 1 + ⌊ − 0.1⌋.]

Now, from the definition of the greatest integer function we have [MATH: ⌊ − 0.1⌋ = − 1.]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: f(− 0.5)|= − 1 + ⌊ − 0.1⌋; = − 1 + (− 1); = − 2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html: Find the value of [MATH: f(x)=(\lceil 6x-3 \rceil -2)^3] at [MATH: x=0.4.]
sections.readable_text: Find the value of [MATH: f(x)=(\lceil 6x-3 \rceil -2)^3] at [MATH: x=0.4.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose that [MATH: x] is a real number. The least integer (or ceiling) function [MATH: \lceil x \rceil] equals the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: \lceil x \rceil = n, \quad\text{where}\quad n-1 \lt x \leq n, \quad n\in\mathbb Z]

Evaluating [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x=0.4,] we get

[MATH: f(0.4)|= (⌈6(0.4) − 3⌉ − 2)^{3}; = (⌈2.4 − 3⌉ − 2)^{3}; = (⌈ − 0.6⌉ − 2)^{3}]

Now, from the definition of the least integer function, we have

[MATH: \lceil -0.6 \rceil = 0.]

Therefore, we conclude that

[MATH: f(0.4)|= (⌈ − 0.6⌉ − 2)^{3}; = (0 − 2)^{3}; = (− 2)^{3}; = − 8.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The greatest integer function (also called the floor function) is denoted

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=\lfloor x \rfloor.]

Content:
This function returns the greatest integer less than or equal to [MATH: x,] where [MATH: x\in\mathbb R.]

Content:
[MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor=n \quad \textrm{where}\quad n \leq x < n+1, \quad n\in\mathbb Z]

Content:
To demonstrate how to evaluate the floor function in practice, let's look at a few different cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: x] is an integer, then [MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor = x{:}]
[MATH: f(6)|= ⌊6⌋ = 6; f(− 2)|= ⌊− 2⌋ = − 2]
- If [MATH: x > 0] but is not an integer, then we simply return the whole number part:
[MATH: f(2.5)|= ⌊2.5⌋ = 2]
- If [MATH: x < 0] but is not an integer, then we subtract one from the whole number part:
[MATH: f(− 3.4)|= ⌊− 3.4⌋ = − 3 − 1 = − 4]

Content:
We can also plot the floor function. According to the definition, we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: ⌊x⌋ = − 2|forx ∈ [− 2, − 1); ⌊x⌋ = − 1|forx ∈ [− 1, 0); ⌊x⌋ = 0|forx ∈ [0, 1); ⌊x⌋ = 1|forx ∈ [1, 2); ⌊x⌋ = 2|forx ∈ [2, 3)]

Content:
And so on. We can use these results to plot the graph of [MATH: f(x)=\lfloor x \rfloor{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c4e52d7a874d03c861cea103249a66ff]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating the Floor Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: f(x)=2x+\left\lfloor \dfrac{x}{5} \right\rfloor,] then what is the value of [MATH: f(-0.5)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose [MATH: x] is a real number. The greatest integer (or floor) function [MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor] equals the greatest integer that is smaller than or equal to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor = n,
\quad\text{where}\quad
n \leq x \lt n+1,\quad n\in \mathbb Z]

Evaluating [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x=-0.5,] we get

[MATH: f(− 0.5)|= 2 ⋅ (− 0.5) + ⌊(− 0.5)/(5)⌋; = − 1 + ⌊ − 0.1⌋.]

Now, from the definition of the greatest integer function we have
[MATH: ⌊ − 0.1⌋ = − 1.]

Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: f(− 0.5)|= − 1 + ⌊ − 0.1⌋; = − 1 + (− 1); = − 2.]

Item 5 — Example: Evaluating the Floor Function in More Complex Cases

Example Prompt:
Find the value of [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{e^{\left\lfloor x+2 \right\rfloor}}{2x+1}] at [MATH: x = 0.75.] Round your answer to [MATH: 2] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose [MATH: x] is a real number. The greatest integer (or floor) function [MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor] equals the greatest integer that is less than or equal to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: \lfloor x \rfloor = n,
\quad\text{where}\quad
n \leq x \lt n+1,\quad n\in \mathbb Z]

Evaluating [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x = 0.75,] we get
[MATH: f(0.75)|= (e^{⌊0.75 + 2⌋})/(2(0.75) + 1); = (e^{⌊2.75⌋})/(2.5).]

Now, from the definition of the greatest integer function, we have
[MATH: \left\lfloor 2.75\right\rfloor = 2.]

Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: f(0.75)|= (e^{⌊2.75⌋})/(2.5); = (e^{2})/(2.5); = 2.95562…; ≈ 2.96,]
rounded to [MATH: 2] decimal places.

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Ceiling Function

Content:
The least integer function (also called the ceiling function) is denoted

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=\lceil x \rceil.]

Content:
This function returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to [MATH: x.] The domain of the ceiling function is [MATH: \mathbb R.]

Content:
[MATH: \lceil x \rceil =n \quad \textrm{where}\quad n-1 < x \leq n, \quad n\in\mathbb Z]

Content:
To demonstrate how to evaluate the ceiling function in practice, let's look at a few different cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: x] is an integer, then [MATH: \lceil x \rceil = x{:}]
[MATH: f(6)|= ⌈6⌉ = 6; f(− 2)|= ⌈− 2⌉ = − 2]
- If [MATH: x > 0] but is not an integer, then we add one to the whole number part:
[MATH: f(2.5)|= ⌈2.5⌉ = 2 + 1 = 3]
- If [MATH: x < 0] but is not an integer, then we simply return the whole number part:
[MATH: f(− 3.4)|= ⌈− 3.4⌉ = − 3]

Content:
We can also plot the ceiling function. According to the definition, we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: ⌈x⌉ = − 2|forx ∈ (− 3, − 2]; ⌈x⌉ = − 1|forx ∈ (− 2, − 1]; ⌈x⌉ = 0|forx ∈ (− 1, 0]; ⌈x⌉ = 1|forx ∈ (0, 1]; ⌈x⌉ = 2|forx ∈ (1, 2]]
And so on. We can use these results to plot the graph of [MATH: f(x)=\lceil x \rceil{:}]

Graphic:

Item 9 — Example: Evaluating the Ceiling Function

Example Prompt:
Find the value of [MATH: f(x)=(\lceil 6x-3 \rceil -2)^3] at [MATH: x=0.4.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose that [MATH: x] is a real number. The least integer (or ceiling) function [MATH: \lceil x \rceil] equals the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: \lceil x \rceil = n,
\quad\text{where}\quad
n-1 \lt x \leq n, \quad n\in\mathbb Z]

Evaluating [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x=0.4,] we get

[MATH: f(0.4)|= (⌈6(0.4) − 3⌉ − 2)^{3}; = (⌈2.4 − 3⌉ − 2)^{3}; = (⌈ − 0.6⌉ − 2)^{3}]

Now, from the definition of the least integer function, we have

[MATH: \lceil -0.6 \rceil = 0.]

Therefore, we conclude that

[MATH: f(0.4)|= (⌈ − 0.6⌉ − 2)^{3}; = (0 − 2)^{3}; = (− 2)^{3}; = − 8.]

Item 12 — Example: Evaluating the Ceiling Function in More Complex Cases

Example Prompt:
Find the value of [MATH: f(x) = \left \lceil e^{6x-5} \right \rceil] at [MATH: x = 1.25.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose that [MATH: x] is a real number. The least integer (or ceiling) function [MATH: \lceil x \rceil] equals the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: \lceil x \rceil = n,
\quad\text{where}\quad
n-1 \lt x \leq n, \quad n\in\mathbb Z]

Evaluating [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x = 1.25,] we get
[MATH: f(1.25)|= ⌈e^{6(1.25) − 5}⌉; = ⌈e^{7.5 − 5}⌉; = ⌈e^{2.5}⌉.]

Now, from the definition of the least integer function, we have
[MATH: \left \lceil e^{2.5} \right \rceil = \left \lceil 12.182\,49 \ldots \right \rceil = 13.]

Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: f(1.25)|= ⌈e^{2.5}⌉; = 13.]
